mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about sp² hybridisation is a common misconception?

options.A: In sp² hybridisation, carbon forms three equivalent sp² hybrid orbitals lying in one plane at 120° angles.
options.B: The remaining unhybridised p orbital is perpendicular to the plane of the sp² hybrids.
options.C: One of the three sp² hybrid orbitals is a pure p orbital.
options.D: sp² hybridisation results in a trigonal planar geometry around the central atom.

mcqs.answer: One of the three sp² hybrid orbitals is a pure p orbital.
mcqs.explanation: In sp² hybridisation one s and two p orbitals combine to give three equivalent sp² hybrid orbitals. All three are hybrids; the remaining p orbital stays pure and is perpendicular to the hybrid plane. Therefore the idea that a hybrid orbital itself is a pure p orbital is a misconception. Options A, B and D correctly describe sp² hybridisation.

mcqs.question: Why does methane (CH₄) adopt a tetrahedral shape as a result of sp³ hybridisation?

options.A: sp³ hybridisation mixes one s and three p orbitals to give four equivalent orbitals arranged at 90° angles.
options.B: The four sp³ hybrid orbitals are directed toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles of 109.5°, which minimizes electron‑pair repulsion.
options.C: In sp³ hybridisation, only three orbitals are used for bonding and the fourth remains a pure p orbital.
options.D: sp³ hybridisation leads to a planar structure with 120° bond angles.

mcqs.answer: The four sp³ hybrid orbitals are directed toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles of 109.5°, which minimizes electron‑pair repulsion.
mcqs.explanation: sp³ hybridisation combines one s and three p orbitals to produce four equivalent hybrid orbitals. These orbitals point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving a bond angle of 109.5° and the most stable arrangement by minimizing repulsion between the four C–H bonds. Option A is wrong about the 90° arrangement, C misstates the number of bonding orbitals, and D describes sp² geometry.

mcqs.question: Which of the following correctly matches each type of hybridisation with its typical molecular geometry and bond angle?

options.A: sp – trigonal planar, 120°; sp² – linear, 180°; sp³ – tetrahedral, 109.5°
options.B: sp – linear, 180°; sp² – trigonal planar, 120°; sp³ – tetrahedral, 109.5°
options.C: sp – tetrahedral, 109.5°; sp² – linear, 180°; sp³ – trigonal planar, 120°
options.D: sp – linear, 180°; sp² – tetrahedral, 109.5°; sp³ – trigonal planar, 120°

mcqs.answer: sp – linear, 180°; sp² – trigonal planar, 120°; sp³ – tetrahedral, 109.5°
mcqs.explanation: sp hybridisation (one s + one p) gives two hybrid orbitals 180° apart → linear geometry. sp² hybridisation (one s + two p) yields three hybrids 120° apart → trigonal planar. sp³ hybridisation (one s + three p) creates four hybrids directed toward the corners of a tetrahedron with a bond angle of 109.5°. Options A, C and D mix the geometries incorrectly.

mcqs.question: Which of the following molecules has the central atom that undergoes sp² hybridisation?
mcqs.explanation: In BF₃, boron uses one s and two p orbitals to form three sp² hybrid orbitals, which lie in one plane and form 120° bond angles with the three fluorine atoms. CH₄ involves sp³ hybridisation, BeCl₂ is linear with sp hybridisation, and NH₃ has sp³ hybridisation (with one lone pair). Hence BF₃ is the correct example of sp² hybridisation.
